body:
**You've rewritten the same task on your to-do list three weeks in a row. You haven't done it. You've just moved it.**

Here's what's actually happening. Every time you defer a task, it doesn't disappear from your brain. It gets filed into a running background process — one that stays open, consuming working memory, generating low-grade stress, every single day you don't close it.

The task itself hasn't gotten harder. But the mental representation of it has. You've rehearsed avoiding it so many times that your brain now has a stronger neural pattern for avoidance than for action.

This is not a discipline problem. It's a pattern problem. And patterns can be interrupted.

The reframe: the task isn't getting bigger. Your brain's prediction of discomfort is getting bigger. Those are not the same thing.

One action: write next to that task the single first physical step — not the goal, the first movement. Open the document. Dial the number. Pull up the file. That's it. Then do only that.

Full breakdown of this system is in the link in bio.
